title: Pressure Cooker vs Slow Cooker: Which Do You Need?
metaDescription: Pressure cooker or slow cooker? How each works, what each is best at, and how to choose the right multi-cooker.
lede: Both make tender, hands-off meals, but in very different ways. One cooks fast under pressure; the other cooks low and slow all day.

p: A pressure cooker seals the pot so steam builds pressure, which raises the boiling point and cooks food much faster. Tough cuts, beans and stocks that take hours on the stove can be done in a fraction of the time.
A slow cooker heats food gently over many hours. You add ingredients in the morning and dinner is ready in the evening.
A pressure cooker suits you if:
list: You decide what to cook at the last minute
You cook dried beans, rice or stock often
You want one appliance with several functions

p: A slow cooker suits you if:
list: You like to prep in the morning and come home to dinner
You want the simplest possible controls
You cook big batches of stews, chili or pulled meat

p: Combo cookers add air frying to a pressure cooker. They're useful if you want crispy results after pressure cooking and have limited counter space, but they are larger and heavier than single-purpose models.
3 quarts suits one or two people, 6 quarts suits most families of up to four, and 7 to 8 quarts suits larger families and batch cooking.

faqs.a: Modern electric pressure cookers include several safety features, such as lid locks and pressure release valves. Follow the manual, keep the valve clean, and never force the lid open.

faqs.q: Can I convert slow cooker recipes for a pressure cooker?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but you'll usually need to reduce cooking time significantly and make sure there's enough liquid for the pot to reach pressure. Recipes written for your specific cooker are the safest starting point.
